Context & Problem
Six steps in,
still no idea what TheFork does.

The existing onboarding puts a new user through six screens — splash, welcome, a three-point "how it works," a tracking pre-permission screen, the ATT system prompt, and a login wall — before they ever see a restaurant or understand what the product is for. Location, the one input that makes the whole value proposition possible ("restaurants near you"), is asked for late and without explanation. The result: users spend the most effort of the entire journey before the app has proven anything to them.

Home & Location
We do not ask for the location, so the first screen already gives us an empty state — negative for the user, who made several steps and finds nothing.
Location's permission
Then, after several steps, we ask for the user's location so we can offer restaurants near them and tell them the value proposition — well after they needed to hear it.
Date & Hour
We are asking a lot of effort from the user, who does not know us yet.
Restaurant listing
After 6 steps, we finally show our listing of different restaurants — based on location, date and hour.

Mission
A first impression strong enough to keep the user — without demanding six steps of faith first.
We don't ask for location, even though it's the key to the one promise we make: restaurants near you. We don't make the path easy or attractive, and we demand a lot of effort from someone who doesn't know us yet. Those pains push the user toward leaving the app — and toward churn — before they've had a reason to stay.

Goal
01
Location
Ask for it in advance, and say why: we want to offer the best deals near you and personalize the search around your best option.
02
Types of food
Get to know the user — cuisine, occasion, budget — to personalize and match against location data first, before offering more.

Value proposition
Once location and food are in, hand back a curated list of nearby restaurants — proof that answering those two questions was worth it.
Wireframes
Structure first, polish after.

Before locking any visual direction, low-fidelity wireframes validated the three-step structure itself — one question per screen, a single primary action, and a visible way out (Skip). Content hierarchy and flow were tested here, before cuisine icons, copy tone or the match-score card design were decided.

The Solution · Shortlist
A quick set of tags become a handpicked list.

[Borrador] The new onboarding personalizes the experience in three simple steps — location, then food preferences — and closes the loop immediately by showing a handpicked Shortlist before the user ever reaches the home screen. Each step explains, in plain language, why the input matters (“find the best spots for you”, “we have many recommendations for you”), so permissions and preferences feel like an exchange, not a tax.

Step 1 · Location
City search or one-tap "Share Location," framed as "Select a city or share location to find the best spots for you" — the value comes before the ask.
Step 2 · Food preferences
Multi-select cuisine chips ("Vegetarian," "Japanese," "Mediterranean"…) that fill in live, so the choice itself feels like the app personalizing in real time.
Step 3 · Shortlist reveal
Before landing on the home feed, the user sees a small, ranked set of restaurants built from what they just told us — proof the previous two steps paid off.
Step 1 · Location  ·  Step 2 · Food preferences
Step 3 · Shortlist reveal  ·  Result · Filtered listing
The ask, then the payoff — value shown before the home screen
Outcome
Projected impact — simulated.
Not measured — this hasn't shipped yet

TheFork Shortlist hasn't launched, so there's no real analytics behind these numbers. What follows is a reasoned projection — built from the specific failure points documented above and typical benchmarks for permission-priming and onboarding-length patterns — not a measured result. It's here to show what I'd expect to move, and why, until the real funnel and permission-grant events are instrumented and this section gets replaced with actual data.

Metric
Old · 6 steps
New · Shortlist
Onboarding completion
Reaches a restaurant listing (vs. abandons mid-flow). Fewer steps and a visible Skip should turn hard drop-offs into soft skips.
~35–45%
~70–80%(est.)
Location permission granted
A value-framed screen before the system prompt ("find the best spots for you") vs. a cold OS dialog with no context.
~30–40%
~55–65%(est.)
Conversion to reservation
From the first screen shown after onboarding — a curated, match-scored Shortlist vs. a generic, unfiltered home feed.
1.0× baseline
~1.3–1.6×(est.)
Launch learnings
Not a number — an open question. Which step or copy line drives the most Skip taps? Does "Share Location" beat typing a city?
To be answered post-launch, per step

Basis for the estimates: shrinking the funnel from 6 screens to 3 removes several points of blind abandonment; priming permission requests with a stated benefit is a well-documented pattern for lifting opt-in versus a cold system prompt; and narrowing a generic feed down to a small, scored, preference-matched set directly targets the decision-fatigue problem named earlier in this case. Ranges are deliberately wide — they're a planning input, not a forecast.
